## Statement

Hazard ratios, odds ratios and model coefficients are routinely presented without naming the intervention, the population, the time horizon or the strategy for each intercurrent event. ICH E9(R1) and the TARGET statement both require that objectives, estimands and sensitivity analyses be aligned, and applied reporting has not caught up. A correctly executed clone-censor-weight analysis with a grace period estimates a marginal contrast between prespecified strategies in the baseline eligible population, and where the artificial censoring enforces adherence that contrast is per-protocol. A bare hazard ratio discloses none of this: not the intervention, not the strategies, not the population, not the horizon, not the handling of intercurrent events. It is therefore read as an intention-to-treat contrast by default, and nothing in the presentation contradicts that reading.

## Why it is open

The hazard ratio survives every methodological improvement beneath it, so better estimation does not change what gets read. Stating the estimand precisely requires naming the strategies and the horizon, and the horizon is a commitment most analyses would rather not defend. The estimand vocabulary and the absolute-risk alternatives both exist and are used in methodological work; what does not exist is a requirement that an applied emulation use them, so the practice is a reporting convention rather than a capability gap.

## What has been tried

::: {.table-scroll}

| Work | What it contributes |
|---|---|
| [ICH E9(R1) addendum on estimands and sensitivity analysis in clinical trials](https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/ich-e9-statistical-principles-clinical-trials-scientific-guideline) | Defines the estimand attributes, population, treatment, endpoint, intercurrent-event strategy and summary measure, that an emulation report would have to fill in. |
| [Hansford HJ, Cashin AG, Jones MD, et al. Transparent reporting of observational studies emulating a target trial: the TARGET statement. JAMA 2025](https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2025.13350) | A 21-item checklist requiring the target protocol and its emulation to be reported, aimed at transparency rather than at risk-of-bias certification. |
| [Maringe C, Benitez Majano S, Exarchakou A, et al. Reflection on modern methods: trial emulation in the presence of immortal-time bias. Int J Epidemiol 2020;49(5):1719-1729](https://doi.org/10.1093/ije/dyaa057) | Makes explicit that clone-censor-weight analyses target per-protocol-type contrasts rather than baseline intention-to-treat effects. |

:::

## Probable solution or research direction

Require a one-sentence estimand statement naming the intervention, the strategies, the population, the horizon and the intercurrent-event handling, positioned before any effect measure. Report absolute risks, risk differences and restricted mean outcomes at clinically meaningful horizons, with the hazard ratio as a supplement rather than the headline. Include a timeline diagram showing treatment paths and censoring rules, since a cloning-and-censoring design is easier to draw than to describe.

## Verification

::: {.verification-trail}
**Verdict.** Unverifiable. Auditors disagreed and the disagreement was evidence-bearing on both sides.

**The source said.** "Hazard ratios, odds ratios and model coefficients are routinely presented without naming the intervention, the population, the time horizon or the strategy for each intercurrent event. ICH E9(R1) and the TARGET statement both require that objectives, estimands and sensitivity analyses be aligned, and applied reporting has not caught up. The concrete failure is specific rather than general: a reader sees a hazard ratio and infers an intention-to-treat contrast, while the analysis in fact estimated a per-protocol effect, weighted for informative censoring, among the subset of patients whose observed treatment stayed compatible with a strategy during a grace period. Those are different quantities in different populations and nothing in the presentation distinguishes them."

**What was wrong with it.** The population named in the original was wrong, and the error matters because it is the error the entry accuses others of. Correct clone-censor weighting does not target the subset whose treatment stayed compatible: the weights reweight uncensored clone-time observations to stand for the artificially censored ones, so the contrast is in the baseline eligible population under the specified strategies. Where censoring enforces adherence the contrast is per-protocol, and the population is still the eligible one.

**Dissent.** literature dissented (open): The estimand vocabulary is arriving in the emulation literature: a 2026 Trials paper applies a hypothetical strategy to the intercurrent event of non-adherence using the parametric g-formula, which is the ICH E9(R1) discipline executed inside a longitudinal analysis, and a 2026 Journal of Epidemiology paper argues explicitly for going beyond the hazard ratio when censoring, confounding and competing events are present. The entry's claim is about what published reports lead with rather than what is possible, and no reporting requirement in the corpus mandates a one-sentence estimand statement or absolute-risk reporting. The presence of these papers means the entry should not imply the vocabulary is missing. codex dissented (overstated): The reporting concern is valid, but the stated population is wrong. Correct clone-censor weighting does not target only patients whose observed treatment remained compatible. It reweights uncensored clone-time observations to represent artificially censored observations, thereby targeting the baseline eligible population under the specified strategies, subject to exchangeability and positivity. A bare hazard ratio identifies neither an intention-to-treat nor a per-protocol strategy and may lack a causal interpretation altogether. TARGET supplies much of the reporting solution; the residual issue is adoption rather than an unresolved estimand method.

Grok 4.5, recency lens
:   **open / supported-with-caveat.** The problem is framed as a presentation/practice failure after standards already exist: a reader sees a bare hazard ratio and infers an intention-to-treat contrast, while the analysis estimated a censoring-weighted per-protocol effect among grace-period–compatible (often cloned) patients. Maringe et al. (IJE 2020; 10.1093/ije/dyaa057), already cited, already makes the CCW estimand type explicit; that formalizes the distinction and does not change what applied papers headline. ICH E9(R1) and the TARGET statement (JAMA 2025; 10.1001/jama.2025.13350) require aligned objectives, estimands, and sensitivity analyses; TARGET item structure places target-trial protocol/estimand items (6a–g) beside emulation mapping (7a–g), and item 13 asks for effect estimates with precision including both absolute and relative measures when applicable. Official TARGET resources confirm that scope and provide protocol table and flow-diagram templates. That is real progress on the reporting-standard side and is the caveat on support: the claim is still true about practice, but “standards are missing” would be overstated after TARGET 2025. What remains open is exactly what the report names: applied reporting has not caught up; the HR remains a familiar default that survives estimator upgrades; and nothing forces a one-sentence estimand that names intervention, population induced by cloning/censoring, horizon, and intercurrent-event strategy before the first effect measure. Fourati et al. (Eur J Prev Cardiol 2026 advance article) still notes that relative measures such as hazard ratios are frequently reported and that absolute risks and risk differences at meaningful times communicate better, which is consistent with ongoing practice lag months after TARGET. No package release (TrialEmulation, gfoRmula, gfoRmulaICE, lmtp, ltmle, survtmle, concrete, riskRegression, adjustedCurves) was found that auto-emits an ICH/TARGET-style estimand sentence or demotes the HR to a supplement. Vote open: standards partially codify the proposed direction; the concrete misread of weighted grace-period PP as ITT HR remains an open practice and communication problem.

glm
:   **open / supported.** The statement is well-scoped and proportionate. It accurately describes the specific mismatch between the reported effect measure (a hazard ratio) and the actual estimand (a per-protocol effect among the grace-period compatible) in clone-censor-weight analyses. The reasons for it being open (cultural inertia of the hazard ratio, difficulty of clinically describing the cloned population, and reluctance to commit to a time horizon for absolute measures) are practical and structural barriers that genuinely support the problem being open.

Decision path
:   `R3:partially-solved(n=1/4) → R7:counter-and-support-both-present(support=1/counter=1)`
